source_text: \'Non fuit\', inquis, \'ordo eiusmodi necessarius, quia statim se et filium et missum et dei Christum rebus ipsis esset probaturus per documenta uirtutum\'. at ego negabo solam hanc illi speciem ad testimonium competisse, quam et, ipse postmodum exauctorauit. siquidem edicens multos uenturos et signa facturos et uirtutes magnas edituros (ad) auersionem etiam electorum, nec ideo tamen admittendos, temerariam signorum et uirtutum fidem ostendit, ut etiam apud pseudochristos facillimarum. aut quale est, si inde se uoluit probari et intellegi et recipi, ex uirtutibus dico, unde ceteros noluit, aeque et ipsos tam subito uenturos quam a nullo auctore praedicatos? si quia prior eis uenit et prior uirtutum documenta signauit, idcirco, quasi locum in balneis, ita fidem occupauit, posteris quibusque praeripuit, uide, ne et ipse in condicione posteriorum deprehendatur, posterior inuentus creatore, ante iam cognito et proinde uirtutes ante operato et non aliter praefato non esse aliis credendum, post eum scilicet. igitur si priorem uenisse et priorem de posteris pronuntiasse hoc fidem t cludet, praedamnatus erit et ipse iam ab eo, quo posterior est agnitus, et solius erit auctoritas creatoris hoc in posteros constituendi, qui nullo posterior * non potuit. iam nunc, cum probaturus sim creatorem easdem uirtutes, quas solas ad fidem Christo tuo uindicas, interdum per famulos suos retro edidisse interdum per Christum suum edendas destinasse, possum et ex hoc merito praescribere tanto magis Christum (tuum) non ex solis uirtutibus credendum fuisse, quanto illum non alterius quam creatoris interpretari potuissent, ut respondentes uirtutibus creatoris et editis per famulos suos et in Christum suum repromissis. quamquam, et si alia documenta inuenirentur in tuo Christo, noua scilicet, facilius crederemus etiam noua eiusdem esse. cuius et uetera, quam cuius tantummodo noua, egentia experimentis fidei uictricis uetustatis, ut sic quoque praedicatus uenire debuerit tam praedicationibus propriis exstruentibus ei fidem quam et uirtutibus. praesertim aduersus Christum creatoris uenturus et signis et prophetiis propriis munitum, ut aemulus Christi per omnes diuersitatum species reluceret. sed quomodo a deo numquam praedicato Christus eius praedicaretur? hoc est ergo, quod exigis: nec deum nec Christum tuum credi, quia et deus ignotus esse non debuit et Christus agnosci per deum debuit.,
pass_a_gloss: You say, 'This kind of order was not necessary, because immediately He would prove Himself and His Son and the one sent and the Christ of God through the very things by means of documents of virtues.' But I will deny that this alone was sufficient for Him as a testimony, which even He Himself later on disavowed. For, in saying that many will come and do signs and produce great virtues, even to the point of aversion of the elect, and yet not be admitted on that account, He shows a rash faith in signs and virtues, just as also among false Christs it is easy. Or what kind is it, if from there He wanted to prove and be understood and be received, I say, from virtues, whence He did not want others, equally and also them, to come so suddenly and be preached by no author? If because He came before them and before them signed the documents of virtues, therefore, as if occupying a place in the baths, so He occupied faith and snatched it away from those who come after, see lest He Himself be caught in the condition of those who come after, found to be after the Creator, and already known before, and therefore having operated virtues before and not otherwise, it should not be believed in others after Him. Therefore, if you declare that the one who came before and pronounced before the others closes faith, He will be condemned beforehand, even by the one by whom He is recognized as after, and the authority will be of the Creator alone to establish this among those who come after, who could not be after no one. Now, since I am about to prove that the Creator did the same virtues, which alone you claim for faith in your Christ, sometimes through His servants having done them before, sometimes having destined them to be done through His Christ, I can also from this merit prescribe that your Christ should not have been believed in from virtues alone, inasmuch as He could have been interpreted as not of another but of the Creator, responding to the virtues of the Creator, both those done through His servants and those promised in His Christ. Although, even if other documents were found in your Christ, namely new ones, we would more easily believe that they too are of the same, lacking experiments of victorious faith of antiquity, so that thus also He ought to have come, preached by His own preachings, building faith for Him, as well as by virtues. Especially since He was to come against the Christ of the Creator, armed with signs and prophecies of His own, so that as a rival of Christ He might shine through all kinds of diversity. But how could the Christ of a God never preached be preached? This, therefore, is what you demand: neither your God nor your Christ should be believed, because God ought not to have been unknown and Christ ought to have been recognized through God.

choices.why: describing the relationship between the two
emphasizing the unknown nature of God
showing the necessary relationship between God and Christ

pass_b_english: You argue that no such sequence was needed, since He would immediately prove Himself, His Son, His envoy, and the Christ of God by the deeds themselves—by the evidence of miracles. I deny that this alone could serve as His credential, a credential He Himself later repudiated. After all, when He declared that many would come performing signs and mighty works—enough to mislead even the elect—and yet insisted they must not be accepted on that basis, He exposed a reckless reliance on signs and wonders, the very currency of false Christs. Consider the logic: if He chose to validate Himself, to be understood and accepted, through miracles, why deny the same grounds to others who arrive just as suddenly and without any prior authorization? If priority of arrival and priority of miraculous attestation let Him seize the faith like a bather claiming a spot in the pool, cutting off all later claimants, watch out—He may find Himself in the same predicament as those He blocks. He was discovered after the Creator, who was already known and had already worked miracles; on that precedent, no one after Him should be believed. So if you rule that the first comer who speaks first on his successors shuts the door on faith, your Christ stands pre-condemned by the very One who identifies Him as the later arrival. The sole authority to set the terms for later claimants belongs to the Creator, who could never be subsequent to anyone. Right now, as I prepare to show that the Creator produced the identical miracles you reserve exclusively for your Christ—sometimes through His servants long ago, sometimes designated for His own Christ—I can legitimately insist that your Christ ought never to have been believed on miracles alone. Those miracles could just as well be read as the Creator’s own, answering to the works He did through His servants and the promises He made in His Christ. Even if novel attestations turned up in your Christ, we would more readily conclude they belong to the same Creator, since your Christ lacks the proven track record of a victorious, ancient faith. That is why He should have come heralded by His own preaching, building faith through proclamation as well as through power. This is especially urgent because He was poised to oppose the Creator’s Christ, armed with his own signs and prophecies, shining as a rival through every kind of difference. But how can the Christ of a God never proclaimed be proclaimed? That is precisely your demand: that neither your God nor your Christ be believed—because God ought not to have remained unknown, and Christ ought to have been recognized through God.
